title: A singleton that survives reflection, serialization and cloning

blocks.text: The page lists the ways a class-based Singleton breaks: **reflection** calls the private constructor, **deserialization** makes a new object, and **cloning** copies it when a superclass exposes `clone()`. Its `SecureSingleton` guards all three, and notes a trap: static initializers run **in textual order**, so a guard flag must be declared (and initialized) **before** the instance.
`Base` (given) implements `Cloneable` and has a public `clone()`. Write `Settings extends Base implements Serializable` so that:

items: Serializing it and reading it back gives **the same instance**.
A second construction through reflection throws `IllegalStateException`.

rows: write then read with object streams

cases.says: Settings.getInstance() returns the same object every time, and its name is settings.
Serializing the instance and reading it back returns the very same instance.
Calling the private constructor through reflection fails with IllegalStateException.
clone(), inherited as public from Base, throws CloneNotSupportedException.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: A Singleton that inherits a public clone() overrides it to throw CloneNotSupportedException.
Deserializing a Singleton creates a new object unless readResolve returns the existing instance.
Static initializers run in textual order, so a guard flag declared after the instance is reset by its own initializer and disables the guard.
